meta.audience: The people of Zarahemla, from the city wall
meta.location: The wall of the city of Zarahemla
principles: A prophet sent back after being refused
A city standing on account of its righteous
Riches that will not stay held

world_behind.title: The preacher is a Lamanite
world_behind.text: Verse 2 names him and his people, and verse 1 has just said the Lamanites keep the law of Moses strictly while the Nephites do not.

world_behind.title: He was already finished and leaving
world_behind.text: Verses 2 and 3 have him cast out, headed home, and turned around by the voice of the Lord. Helaman 10:12 has Nephi make the same turn a few chapters earlier, stopping short of his own house and going back. Two prophets in this book are sent back to a city that has just refused them.

world_behind.title: The wall is a workaround
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says they would not suffer him to enter the city, so he got upon the wall. Helaman 7:10 puts Nephi on a tower in his own garden and Alma 31:13 puts the Zoramites on a raised stand; the record keeps noting where a speaker had to stand to be heard.

world_behind.title: The four hundred years are dated
world_behind.text: Verses 5 and 9 give the interval twice, and verse 10 says men of the fourth generation among his enemies will see the destruction.

world_behind.title: Zarahemla is standing on borrowed time
world_behind.text: Verses 12 and 13 say the righteous are the reason it is spared, and verse 14 gives the moment it will be ripe: when they cast the righteous out.

world_behind.title: The curse on riches is stated in full
world_behind.text: Verses 18 through 23 and 31 through 36 describe treasures that cannot be found and tools that vanish overnight.

world_behind.title: The lament is written out in advance
world_behind.text: Verses 33 through 37 give the words the people will say afterwards, and verse 37 ends them mid-prayer. Mormon 2:10 to 14 reports that lament actually being spoken four hundred years later, and calls it the sorrowing of the damned rather than repentance.

words.text: News, especially good news. The record uses the word twenty-two times and the King James Bible forty-six. Verse 7 has an angel bringing glad tidings to Samuel, who was sent to pass them on and was refused.
Clothing, in the record usually costly clothing. The word occurs fourteen times, often as a marker of pride, as at Alma 1:6 and Alma 4:6. Verse 28 has it given to a man who says all is well.
Turned away from what is right. The record uses the word six times and the King James Bible twenty. Samuel pairs it with hardened and stiffnecked in a single address.
Set alight. The record uses the word five times and the King James Bible sixty-six, nearly always of anger. Verse 30 says the anger is already kindled, in the past tense.
Unable to be held. The record uses the word four times, three of them in this chapter and one at Mormon 1:18, where Mormon reports it happening. The King James Bible has it three times, of paths.
Evil spirits. The word occurs once in all of scripture, here, inside the lament Samuel puts in their mouths.

phrases.term: There was one Samuel, a Lamanite, came into the land of Zarahemla
phrases.text: The record introduces its only named Lamanite prophet in a single clause. Verse 1 has already reported which people was keeping the law.

phrases.term: He went and got upon the wall thereof
phrases.text: The improvisation that makes the chapter possible. Shut out of the city, he preaches from its boundary.

phrases.term: Four hundred years pass not away save the sword of justice falleth upon this people
phrases.text: The interval given at the start of the sermon. Verse 9 repeats it, and Mormon writes the abridgment from the far side of it.

phrases.term: It is because of those who are righteous that it is saved
phrases.text: The reason the city still stands. Verse 13 says fire from heaven would otherwise have come down.

phrases.term: When ye shall cast out the righteous from among you, then shall ye be ripe for destruction
phrases.text: The condition that ends the reprieve. The city's protection is a group of people it can decide to expel.

phrases.term: Whoso shall hide up treasures in the earth shall find them again no more
phrases.text: The curse stated as law. Helaman 12:18 had given the principle, and this verse extends it over the whole land.

phrases.term: Ye do always remember your riches, not to thank the Lord your God for them
phrases.text: The distinction between remembering a thing and remembering its source. Verse 22 lists what fills the space instead: pride, boasting, envyings, strifes, malice, persecutions, murders.

phrases.term: If our days had been in the days of our fathers of old, we would not have slain the prophets
phrases.text: The claim Samuel quotes back at them. Verse 26 answers it by describing what they do to a prophet who is standing in front of them.

phrases.term: Because he speaketh flattering words unto you, and he saith that all is well
phrases.text: The test the people actually use. A man who says there is no iniquity gets gold, silver, and costly apparel.

phrases.term: He curseth your riches, that they become slippery, that ye cannot hold them
phrases.text: The image the chapter is remembered by. Mormon 1:18 reports it as an ordinary fact of daily life three centuries later.

phrases.term: Ye have sought for happiness in doing iniquity
phrases.text: The summary of the whole failure. Alma 41:10 had put it in four words to his own son.

verses.label: v. 4
verses.title: One clause of staging that shapes the rest
verses.text: The record explains the pulpit before it reports a word: "they would not suffer that he should enter into the city; therefore he went and got upon the wall thereof." Everything after follows from that sentence. The preacher is outside, above, and unable to be reached, which is why the chapter ends with him still speaking and why the next chapter can have people shooting at him. A sermon delivered from a city wall by a man of the enemy nation is a different act from the same words spoken indoors, and the record supplies the difference in a single subordinate clause.

verses.label: v. 5–7
verses.title: Three links, stated before any content
verses.text: The record sets out the chain that carries the message before it gives any of the message. The Lord "doth put into my heart" (v. 5), then "an angel of the Lord hath declared it unto me, and he did bring glad tidings to my soul" (v. 7), then "I was sent unto you to declare it unto you" (v. 7). Source, courier, errand. The speaker also names himself twice in three verses, "I, Samuel, a Lamanite," which is the only self-identification in the sermon and the fact his audience would find hardest to accept.

verses.label: v. 8–29
verses.title: A sermon built out of two words
verses.text: Will stands twenty-eight times in this chapter and every use falls between verses 8 and 29. Only two chapters of scripture use it more. Because stands nineteen times across fifteen verses, second among the eight hundred and four chapters that use it at all, and it too stops at verse 35. One word puts the whole sermon in the future and the other supplies a reason for every item in it. Strip both and almost nothing of the argument survives, because the argument is entirely a chain of causes running forward.

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: A number repeated across sixty-eight years
verses.text: "Four hundred years shall not pass away before I will cause that they shall be smitten." The phrase four hundred years stands in four verses of the volume: Alma 45:10, this verse and verse 5 here, and Morm. 8:6. Alma gave the figure about sixty-eight years before Samuel does, anchoring it to the coming of Christ; Samuel anchors it to his own day. Mormon 8:6 is the fourth, written by a man reporting that the term has run out. A reader can line up all four and check that the arithmetic holds.

verses.label: v. 18–20
verses.title: A curse described as a property of objects
verses.text: Hide is used seven times in three verses and nowhere else in the chapter. What the curse does is not stated as punishment but as behaviour belonging to things: "whoso shall hide up treasures in the earth shall find them again no more, because of the great curse of the land." Verse 19 supplies the exception, treasures hidden "unto me," and verse 20 the diagnosis, "because they have set their hearts upon riches." Later verses extend it to tools and swords, and slippery becomes the word for it, standing in three verses here and returning once more in the volume at Morm. 1:18.

verses.label: v. 25–28
verses.title: The audience's own excuse, quoted and then answered
verses.text: The sermon puts a sentence in its hearers' mouths: "If our days had been in the days of our fathers of old, we would not have slain the prophets; we would not have stoned them." The same move appears at Matt. 23:30, where the wording is "If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets." What follows here is not the reply Matthew gives. Instead of calling them the children of the killers, verses 26 to 28 describe what they in fact do with two kinds of preacher, and let the contrast between the true prophet cast out and the flatterer clothed in costly apparel stand as the refutation.

verses.label: v. 32–37
verses.title: Six verses of speech that nobody has said yet
verses.text: The record gives a long passage of first-person lament and attributes it to the future: "in that day ye shall say: O that we had remembered the Lord our God." Five more verses continue in the same voice, complaining about a tool laid down and gone by morning, swords missing on the day of battle, treasures that have slipped away. This is direct discourse with no speaker, quoted in advance from people who will be sorry. Then verse 38 drops the device and addresses the living: "your days of probation are past."

chapter.title: The prophet was already leaving
chapter.text: Verses 2 and 3 have him finished and turned around. Everything in the chapter happens after the point where a reasonable person would have gone home.

chapter.title: The wall is the sermon's setting and its argument
chapter.text: He is outside because they put him there, and he preaches from the boundary of a city he was not allowed into.

chapter.title: A Lamanite preaches to the Nephites
chapter.text: Verse 1 sets up the reversal Helaman 6 had already reported. The messenger's identity is part of the message.

chapter.title: The city is spared for its minority
chapter.text: Verses 12 through 14 make the righteous the reason it stands and their expulsion the moment it falls. Genesis 18 had put the same arithmetic to Abraham.

chapter.title: The test for a prophet is comfort
chapter.text: Verses 26 through 28 describe people who reward the man who says all is well. Samuel names the mechanism rather than only the outcome.

chapter.title: The curse works on holding, not on having
chapter.text: Verse 31 does not take the riches away; it makes them impossible to keep. Mormon 1:18 reports tools and treasures vanishing as normal life.

chapter.title: The lament is supplied in advance
chapter.text: Verses 33 through 37 are written in their future voice. Samuel gives them the words and tells them this will be their language.

chapter.title: He ends with a prayer for them
chapter.text: Verse 39 follows the sentence that it is everlastingly too late. The chapter closes on the wish rather than on the verdict.

applications.title: Go back when you are sent back
applications.text: He had preached, been refused, and started home, and the instruction was to return. A closed door is sometimes not the end of the assignment.

applications.title: Preach from the wall
applications.text: Barred from the city, he used its boundary. When the ordinary access is denied, look for the position that still lets the work happen.

applications.title: Remember the warning was meant as good news
applications.text: Samuel says an angel brought glad tidings to his soul and that he came so they could have them too. A message that lands as a rebuke was often sent as an offer, and the hearing decides which one it becomes.

applications.title: A few people can be why a place stands
applications.text: The city is spared for the sake of the righteous who are in it. Whatever you think of your own influence, being present somewhere is a contribution this record is willing to count.

applications.title: Distrust the story in which you would have done better
applications.text: They said that had their days been in their fathers' days, they would not have slain the prophets. A confident account of how you would have acted in a past you did not live through is flattering and untested.

applications.title: Watch who you reward for telling you things
applications.text: They paid the man who said all is well. Notice which messengers you fund and which you resent.

applications.title: Hold your holdings loosely
applications.text: The curse was on keeping rather than on having. Anything you are counting on to stay put is worth examining while it is still in hand.

applications.title: Name the delay as the decision
applications.text: The charge here is procrastination of the day of salvation rather than any outright refusal. Postponing something long enough is a way of choosing it, and it never feels like the moment you chose.

questions.text: What was I about to give up on that I have been told to resume?
Who is keeping the place I live standing?
Do I remember the gift or the giver?
What would I claim I would have done in someone else's era?
Whose true words about me have I called unfair?
What comfortable voice am I paying for?
What would I say if I lost what I am holding onto now?

targets.verse_text: And behold, if a man hide up a treasure in the earth, and the Lord shall say—Let it be accursed, because of the iniquity of him who hath hid it up—behold, it shall be accursed.
targets.markdown: And behold, **if a man hide up a treasure in the earth**, and the Lord shall say—Let it be accursed, because of the iniquity of him who hath hid it up—behold, it shall be accursed.
